notes: Section 72 challenge to fraudulent arbitration award; service, jurisdiction and Article 10 analysis are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Arab National Bank v El-Abdali: fraudulent arbitration award set aside
key_facts: The Arab National Bank challenged a purported $160 million arbitration award and mortgage purportedly made by HRH Prince Adel El-Hashemite in favour of Mr El-Abdali.
The Bank denied any arbitration agreement, proper tribunal constitution or valid acknowledgment of proceedings; it said signatures on acknowledgment and mortgage documents were forged.
The underlying dispute arose from Saudi banking services and was already before SAMA; the Prince's communications came without proper arbitral procedure.
Forum Law had previously agreed to accept service of injunctive proceedings but did not defend the claim at trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court trial of an arbitration claim under section 72 of the Arbitration Act 1996 for declarations and injunctions.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted that the purported award and mortgage were not binding or enforceable; injunctions granted restraining enforcement and publication, with the hearing held in public.
enrichment.ratio: A non-participating party may bring section 72 proceedings where England is the seat of the arbitration; a solicitor who has agreed to accept service of injunctive proceedings is duly authorized for service under CPR 6.4, and Article 10 does not prevent injunctive protection of reputation against publication of a manifestly fraudulent award.
legal_issues: Whether proceedings were validly served on the defendant's solicitors
Whether the court had jurisdiction under section 72 given dispute over the seat
Whether there was a valid arbitration agreement and properly constituted tribunal
Whether injunctions restraining publication were compatible with Article 10 and section 12 HRA
linked_authorities: Department of Economics, Policy and Development of the City of Moscow v Bankers Trust Co [2004] 3 WLR 533
Nanglegan v Royal Free Hampstead NHS Trust [2002] 1 WLR 1043
Union of India v McDonnell Douglas Corporation [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 48

notes: Sheffield firearms gang sentencing appeals; Docking reduction and refusal of co-appellants' appeals are clear.

enrichment.short_title: R v Docking and others: Sheffield gun crime sentencing appeals
key_facts: Wild, Lewis and Cook were convicted of conspiracies to cause grievous bodily harm and commit criminal damage after a balaclava attack on Fletcher involving a loaded shotgun.
Docking separately attempted to murder Lewis in a reprisal drive-by shooting and dangerous high-speed pursuit through Sheffield.
Witness intimidation meant key evidence was unreliable; Allen was acquitted after witnesses failed to attend.
Docking had a substantial record and was on licence; the judge passed deterrent sentences reflecting recent gun crime in Sheffield.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal criminal appeals against sentence following Sheffield Crown Court convictions.
enrichment.outcome: Docking's total sentence was reduced from twenty to sixteen years by substituting sixteen years for attempted murder and making dangerous driving concurrent; renewed applications by Wild, Lewis and Cook were refused.
enrichment.ratio: The firearms sentencing tariff has increased since White and Avis; an eighteen-year starting point for attempted murder with a loaded shotgun on licence was not manifestly excessive, though a consecutive term for dangerous driving made the total twenty-year sentence excessive.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentence for attempted murder involving firearms
Whether dangerous driving should run consecutively to attempted murder
Whether eight and fourteen-year sentences for conspiracy to cause GBH were manifestly excessive
Effect of witness intimidation and limited mitigation on sentencing
linked_authorities: R v White 13 Cr App R (S) 108
R v Avis [1998] 2 Cr App R (S) 178
R v Gouldthorpe [2004] 1 Cr App R (S) 248

notes: Case stated on proof of restraining order; strict liability and interview admissions clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Barber v CPS: proving a restraining order by interview admission
key_facts: Mr Barber was convicted of breaching a restraining order by playing loud bass music causing distress to the Prosser family.
The prosecution did not produce a formal copy of the order but relied on interview admissions and witness references to its existence.
The magistrates wrongly treated the offence as requiring proof of mens rea but accepted the interview as proving the order.
The appellant argued the order and its terms had not been proved to the criminal standard.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from South Worcestershire Justices.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; breach of a restraining order is strict liability and the order was properly proved by admissible interview admissions.
enrichment.ratio: An offence under section 5(5) of the 1997 Act is one of strict liability; proof of the restraining order need not follow Rule 68 formally and may be established by a confession in interview capable of admission under section 76 PACE.
legal_issues: Whether breach of a restraining order is an offence of strict liability
Whether Rule 68 required formal production of the order
Whether the police interview amounted to an admission of the order and its terms
Whether the magistrates were entitled to convict on the evidence adduced

notes: Long-running section 19A penalty appeal; statutory finality and compliance date analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Murat v Revenue: penalties for failure to comply with section 19A notice
key_facts: Mr Murat, a chartered accountant, failed to produce documents including a balance sheet required by a section 19A notice following an enquiry into his 1996/97 return.
He had unsuccessfully appealed the notice itself before Special Commissioner Dr Brice in May 2000.
Penalties totalling substantial sums were imposed for non-compliance by 8 July 2000, calculated as thirty days after Dr Brice's 8 June determination.
Mr Murat argued the penalty notices were defective, self-incriminating and breached Articles 3, 4 and 14 ECHR.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal in law under section 56(6) TMA against a Special Commissioner's dismissal of penalty appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; penalty notices specified the correct compliance date and the taxpayer could not reopen the section 19A requirement; ECHR arguments rejected; costs assessed at £3,000.
enrichment.ratio: A determination on appeal against a section 19A notice is final under section 19A(11), so penalty proceedings cannot reopen the underlying requirement; under section 19A(10) the compliance period runs thirty days from the date the determination is made, not from receipt by the taxpayer.
legal_issues: Whether penalty proceedings could challenge the original section 19A notice
Construction of section 19A(10) and the correct compliance deadline
Whether requiring a balance sheet infringed Article 6 self-incrimination rights
Whether Articles 3, 4 and 14 were engaged
linked_authorities: Accountant v Her Majesty's Inspector of Taxes SpC00258
Van Der Musselle v Belgium [1983] 6 EHRR 163

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and dismissal on each ECHR point are clearly expressed.

notes: Assault by penetration sentence appeal under Sexual Offences Act 2003; Garvey starting point applied.

enrichment.short_title: R v Minshull: sentence for assault by penetration of vulnerable child
key_facts: The applicant pleaded guilty to assault by penetration of a thirteen-year-old girl with severe learning difficulties who was partially sighted and deaf.
He was a friend of the victim's father and digitally penetrated the girl in the bathroom while briefly left alone with her.
The victim's DNA was found on his hand; he had prior convictions for indecent assault on under-fourteens in 1996.
The judge adopted a seven-year starting point before credit for plea, passing five years' imprisonment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for leave to appeal against sentence referred to the Full Court.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; five-year sentence upheld as unimpeachable given aggravating features.
enrichment.ratio: Following Attorney-General's Reference No 140 of 2004 (Garvey), the ordinary starting point for adult assault by penetration is about four years, but age, vulnerability, breach of trust and previous convictions can justify a seven-year starting point before plea discount.
legal_issues: Appropriate starting point for assault by penetration under the 2003 Act
Relevance of prior indecent assault convictions and breach of trust
Whether pre-2003 indecent assault sentencing authorities remained authoritative
Effect of the victim's learning and sensory disabilities
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's Reference No 140 of 2004 (Garvey)
R v Milberry [2003] 1 Cr App R (S) 396

confidence.notes: Aggravating features, Garvey starting point and refusal of leave are clearly stated.

notes: Indefinite driving ASBO varied to two years; P principles and sentencing context are clear.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hall: indefinite ASBO for serial disqualified driving reduced
key_facts: Hall pleaded guilty to driving while disqualified, dangerous driving, no insurance and failing to stop after police recognised him in a lay-by.
He led police on an eighty mph pursuit through a give-way junction, weaving through traffic until crashing into street furniture.
The Crown Court imposed twelve months' imprisonment and an indefinite ASBO prohibiting driving without licence and insurance, with breach carrying up to five years.
Hall had an extensive history of disqualified driving and related motoring offences from age ten.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against an ASBO imposed alongside a Crown Court motoring sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed only to limit the ASBO duration to two years from July 2004; twelve-month custodial sentence untouched.
enrichment.ratio: An ASBO may properly address repeated serious driving offending that amounts to anti-social behaviour if its terms are precise and explained in open court under R v P, but an indefinite order is inappropriate where a fixed term better balances public protection with the offender's ability to comply.
legal_issues: Whether an ASBO was necessary for driving offences
Whether the order followed the principles in R v P
Whether an indefinite ASBO was appropriate
Whether the ASBO was improperly used to increase maximum penalty for driving while disqualified
linked_authorities: R v P [2004] EWCA Crim (Feb 2004)

confidence.notes: Limited allowance on duration only; P principles and offending history are explicit.

notes: Ghafoor age-threshold DTO appeal; supervision substitution and Article 7 analysis are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: R v NH: Ghafoor limits on detention and training orders
key_facts: At fourteen the appellant recklessly accepted oral sex from an eighteen-year-old woman with learning difficulties during a group incident in Streatham.
He was not present for the initial coercion or theft of the phone and pleaded on an agreed limited basis.
Sentenced at fifteen to a twelve-month detention and training order although he was not a persistent offender and could not have received custody at fourteen.
Judge Grobel treated the seriousness of the offence as justification for departing from the Ghafoor starting point.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal against a detention and training order imposed on guilty plea.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; twelve-month DTO quashed and replaced with twelve months' supervision including ninety days' specified activities, electronic curfew and community requirements.
enrichment.ratio: Under Ghafoor, where an offender crosses the age-15 threshold between offence and conviction the starting point is the sentence likely at the date of offence; seriousness alone cannot justify departing from that starting point or imposing a DTO unavailable at the time of the offence.
legal_issues: Application of section 100(2) to offenders aged under 15 at conviction
Whether seriousness could justify departure from the Ghafoor starting point
Whether Article 7 ECHR was engaged
Appropriate non-custodial sentence for the agreed basis of plea
linked_authorities: R v Ghafoor [2002] EWCA Crim 1857
R v LM [2003] 2 Cr App R (S) 26
R v Jones [2003] Crim LR 639

notes: Cohabitee resulting trust appeal dismissed; purchase-price contribution principles clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Curley v Parkes: resulting trust claim after cohabitation purchase
key_facts: Andrew Curley cohabited with Nicola Parkes and claimed a fifty-percent beneficial interest in 117 Battalion Drive bought in her sole name.
The judge found no express or inferred common intention constructive trust; mortgage and household costs were paid from a joint account.
Curley received relocation payments from Vauxhall and later paid Miss Parkes instalments said to compensate her deposit, plus solicitors' and removal costs.
On appeal the only live issue was whether those payments were contributions to the purchase price for a resulting trust.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on permission limited to whether the county court judge failed to consider a resulting trust.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; post-completion payments and relocation-related expenses were not purchase-price contributions and no resulting trust arose.
enrichment.ratio: A resulting trust crystallises at acquisition and looks to contributions to the purchase price; subsequent payments, including reimbursement of deposit and costs paid after completion, do not create a resulting trust unless they were part of the purchase price at the date of acquisition.
legal_issues: Whether post-completion payments to the legal owner were contributions to purchase price
Whether solicitors' fees and removal costs paid via a relocation scheme counted
Whether mortgage instalments from a joint account could support a resulting trust
Effect of the judge's failure to address the resulting trust argument
linked_authorities: Marsh v von Sternberg [1986] 1 FLR 526
Huntingford v Hobbs [1993] 1 FLR 736

confidence.notes: Limited appeal ground and detailed rejection of each claimed contribution are clear.

notes: Green Belt gypsy site permission challenge failed; special educational needs and personal condition reasoning detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Dartford v SoS: Green Belt gypsy site and special educational needs
key_facts: William Lee sought permanent planning permission for six caravans for three related families on Green Belt land at Sutton-at-Hone.

An inspector recommended refusal but the Secretary of State redetermined after quashing an earlier decision and granted personal permission relying on unmet gypsy site need and the Lee children's special educational needs.
Head teachers provided evidence that disruption would be educationally disastrous for children with severe learning difficulties already supported locally.
Dartford challenged the personal permission extending to all three families and the adequacy of reasons on educational needs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 challenge to a redetermined planning appeal decision granting Green Belt permission.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; very special circumstances were adequately reasoned and personal permission for the extended family reflected how the case was presented.
enrichment.ratio: Children's normal educational needs alone may not be very special circumstances, but detailed evidence of special educational needs currently met at local schools can combine with unmet gypsy accommodation need to outweigh Green Belt harm; a personal condition may extend to an extended family where the case was brought on that basis and no planning reason required restricting caravans to one family.
legal_issues: Whether special educational needs amounted to very special circumstances in the Green Belt
Whether personal planning permission for three families was justified
Adequacy of the Secretary of State's reasons after written representations
Distinction from R (Chelmsford BC) v First Secretary of State
linked_authorities: R (Chelmsford BC) v First Secretary of State and Draper [2003] EWHC 2978 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Fact-sensitive planning judgment with extensive reasoning; outcome turns on case presentation as well as educational evidence.

notes: Major RTA quantum judgment; earnings, patient status and lifetime care fund fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Dixon v Were: severe brain injury damages after RTA
key_facts: Simon Dixon suffered severe traumatic brain injury and multiple orthopaedic injuries when a drunk-driven car hit a tree in July 1997, killing two passengers.
Liability was admitted subject to twenty-seven and a half percent contributory negligence for failing to wear a seat belt.
He developed an organic personality disorder and bipolar affective disorder, leaving him unemployable and requiring structured care and case management.
Past losses of £345,000 and general damages of £147,500 were agreed; the trial resolved future earnings, patient status and a lifetime care fund.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of quantum in a road traffic personal injury action after partial admissions.
enrichment.outcome: Substantial future awards made including about £905,000 for earnings and car allowance, Court of Protection costs, and about £2.24 million for care; total past and future loss about £4.18 million before contributory negligence reduction to about £3.03 million.
enrichment.ratio: Future loss of earnings for a young student should reflect realistic financial-sector prospects rather than bare national averages; under Masterman-Lister capacity is issue-specific so a claimant may lack capacity to manage a large damages fund though litigation capacity differs; a resulting care fund should target reasonable lifetime needs without over-engineering percentage discounts already built into the multiplicand.
legal_issues: Appropriate career model and multiplicands for future loss of earnings
Whether loss of a chance of very high earnings was speculative
Whether the claimant remained a patient for litigation and fund management
Reasonable level of support workers, case management and hospital admissions
linked_authorities: Herring v Ministry of Defence [2003] EWCA Civ 528
Masterman-Lister v Brutton & Co [2003] 1 WLR 1511
Woodrup v Nicol [1993] PIQR Q104
